newsitem.title: TURKMENISTAN: Shell hold talks with Turkmenistan on gas pipeline.
newsitem.headline: Shell hold talks with Turkmenistan on gas pipeline.

text.p: Turkmen President Saparmurat Niyazov met a top representative of Anglo-Dutch oil major Royal Dutch Shell last week to discuss building a gas pipeline from Turkmenistan to Turkey and southern Europe via Iran, a Turkmen Foreign Ministry source said on Tuesday.

The source, who asked to remain anonymous, said the meeting took place on Thursday and was attended by Britain's ambassador to Turkmenistan, Neil Hook, and the president of Shell EP International Ventures BV, Allan John Parsley.
"Shell is looking at investing significant amounts in Turkmenistan, and London can only officially welcome that," Hook told Reuters.
Shell was not immediately available for official comment on the talks and its Turkmen projects in general.

The Foreign Ministry source said last week's talks were in line with a memorandum of understanding to build a natural gas pipeline which was signed in Ashgabat in May by the presidents of Turkey, Turkmenistan and Iran.
The memorandum outlined plans for Turkmenistan to export up to 28-30 billion cubic metres of gas annually for 30 years, and the cost of the project was provisionally pegged at $1.6 billion.
Iran said in May it would provide the export route across its territory to the Turkish border, while Turkey said it would ensure markets were found for the gas.
New gas export routes will be vital to Turkmenistan's long-term economic revival, because it now depends entirely on Russian gas pipelines to get its "blue gold" to hard currency markets in Europe.
Relations between Niyazov and Rem Vyakhirev, chief executive of Russia's natural gas monopoly Gazprom, have been soured by the collapse of an export deal the two sides reached late last year.

With no alternative routes or markets for its huge natural gas reserves, Turkmen gas output and sales, by far the impoverished Central Asian state's biggest hard currency earner, have dropped sharply this year.
In a letter addressed to Niyazov and published in the official Turkmen press, Shell said it was most interested in taking part in a project that would supply Turkmen gas to profitable markets.
"The size of the company and its unique international character would successfully suit the scale of the project and the political neutrality of Turkmenistan," the letter said.
Shell, the National Iranian Oil Company (NIOC) and the Turkmen government also agreed at last week's talks to set up a joint venture, the Foreign Ministry source said.
The venture, which has yet to be officially formed, plans to develop offshore oil and gas deposits in an area around the Caspian border between Iran and Turkmenistan.
Shell's Parsley said on Turkmen national television that Shell also intended to take part in an international tender for developing oil and gas reserves on the Turkmen sector of the Caspian shelf.

Shell officials have said the company is keen to raise its profile in the resource-rich Caspian region, having lost out to other international oil majors which have already succeeded in taking part in multi-billion-dollar oil ventures.
The Turkmen offshore tender opens on September 1 and the results are due to be announced by January 1.
